\chapter{Describing Things}
\label{ch:kn-describing-things}
\hlchaptermodality{42}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something in Kannada and ask who or where it is — and I can say what the six words have in common.}

Say the near word, the far word and the question word in a row, and name the part that changed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[doḍḍa]{\kn{ದೊಡ್ಡ} (doḍḍa) — big}

\label{lesson:KA-C42-big}



\begin{quote}
You can already name things. This is how you POINT at them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ದೊಡ್ಡ}}
\textbf{\kn{ದೊಡ್ಡ}} — \emph{doḍḍa} — big.

Put it in front of a word you already know and you have said something new. That is all an adjective does in this language.

The last lesson of this chapter gives the one rule that governs every adjective you will ever meet here.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}\kn{ದೊಡ್ಡ}\textquotedblright{} three times, pointing at something different each time
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once with a word you already know after it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kāphi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{doḍḍa}? (\textbf{big}.) Where does it go — before the word it describes, or after? (\textbf{Before.})
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[before the noun, unchanged]{before the noun, unchanged — five words, one rule}

\label{lesson:KA-C42-adjective-system}



\begin{quote}
Say the five words from this chapter out loud, then say each one in front of a noun you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: where an adjective goes}]
You did not learn five separate words. You learned \textbf{where an adjective goes}, and five words that go there.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
big & \textbf{\kn{ದೊಡ್ಡ}} \emph{doḍḍa} \\
small & \textbf{\kn{ಚಿಕ್ಕ}} \emph{cikka} \\
good & \textbf{\kn{ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ}} \emph{oḷḷeya} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They sit in front of the noun and stay exactly as they are.

This is worth more than the five words are. Every noun you already know — your name, the house, the water, the day — can now take any of them in front, and every adjective you meet from here goes in the same place.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} each of the five in front of a noun you already know
  \item \emph{Say it:} two of them with the same noun, one after the other
  \item \emph{Notice:} whether the adjective changed shape when the noun did
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does an adjective go in this language? (\textbf{In front of the noun.}) Does it change shape to match the noun? (unchanged.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ña]{\kn{ಞ} — one character, and the stack it hides in}

\label{lesson:KA-S133-letter-nya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌ಃ} — what does it add, and which mark is its partner?

One character this time. You will hardly ever see it alone, and that fact is the lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಞ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಞ}} — \emph{ña}.

It is a \textbf{nasal}, and you can already read two of its relatives:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನ}} \emph{na} — tongue at the teeth ridge, the sound in \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra}
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಣ}} \emph{ṇa} — tongue curled back, the sound in \textbf{\kn{ಗಂಟೆ}} \emph{gaṇṭe}
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಞ}} \emph{ña} — tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, the \emph{ny} an English speaker hears in \textbf{canyon}
\end{itemize}

Kannada keeps these apart as separate letters where English writes \emph{n} for all three and lets the neighbours decide.

\textbf{Why you will not see it standing.} Almost every time it appears it is \textbf{stacked underneath another letter}. The pair you will meet is:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಜ}} plus \textbf{\kn{ಞ}} stacked gives \textbf{\kn{ಜ್ಞ}}
\end{itemize}

Learn that stack, because it is where this letter lives, and a word built on it is close at hand. Find the \textbf{\kn{ಜ}} on top; what is squashed underneath is today's character. Expect it under another letter, not beside one.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಞ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಞ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these three nasals and say which one is today's
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನ}  ·  \kn{ಣ}  ·  \kn{ಞ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಞ} three times, saying \emph{ña} as in canyon as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಜ್ಞ} and say which letter sits on top and which is squashed beneath
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three nasals in a row — \textquotedblleft{}na, ṇa, ña\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಞ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ña}}, the \emph{ny} of \textbf{canyon}.) Where will you nearly always find it? (\textbf{Stacked underneath another letter}, as in \textbf{\kn{ಜ್ಞ}}.) Name the two nasals you could already read. (\textbf{\kn{ನ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಣ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
